title: The Gang Runs for Office

jokes.text: Characters are enthusiastically admiring Garbage Pail Kids cards — 'Heavin' Steven' — as priceless collectibles
jokes.setup: Two grown men are excitedly hunched over a card collection like children
jokes.punchline: The cards are Garbage Pail Kids — deliberately disgusting novelty cards for children — treated with the reverence of fine art
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP character comedy — grown men treating juvenile garbage as treasure. 'Heavin' Steven' as a specific named card adds texture. Works because it immediately characterizes the gang's arrested development.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Are those those stupid cards where babies are doing disgusting things?' Mac: 'Uh, no. They're the amazing cards where babies are doing hysterical things.'
jokes.setup: Dee dismisses the cards as stupid and gross
jokes.punchline: Mac's rebuttal is structurally identical to her description — same content, just reframed as positive — which only confirms how ridiculous they are
jokes.explanation: Very economical and well-structured. The joke works because Mac's correction is structurally indistinguishable from Dee's insult — 'stupid/disgusting' vs 'amazing/hysterical' — exposing his delusion through perfect parallel construction. Tight, funny, character-specific.

jokes.text: Charlie insists his Garbage Pail Kids are 'an investment' and 'my future here'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to buy some of Charlie's cards
jokes.punchline: Charlie treats his Garbage Pail Kid collection as a serious financial investment and his retirement plan
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — Charlie's delusional financial reasoning is very on-brand. Gets rewatch bonus because this setup pays off huge when he trades the whole collection for the smear tape later. The investment framing makes the eventual trade more painful and funnier.

jokes.text: Mac reads: 'We are getting blasted in the ass by the state liquor tax.' Dennis: '"Blasted in the ass"?'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to make a serious political point about taxes
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'blasted in the ass' derails the conversation immediately — Dennis can't get past the sexual connotation
jokes.explanation: Functional juvenile humor. The double entendre is obvious but the delivery works. Sets up the escalating 'ass blast' riff that follows.

jokes.text: The gang escalates 'ass blast' into full political philosophy: 'Am I supposed to vote for the Democrat who's gonna blast me in the ass or the Republican who's blasting my ass? Politics is just one big ass blast. It is a coast-to-coast, nationwide ass blast.'
jokes.setup: What started as an accidental double entendre becomes their entire political worldview
jokes.punchline: The metaphor escalates to 'coast-to-coast, nationwide ass blast' — a fully articulated political philosophy built entirely on a crude euphemism
jokes.explanation: The escalation from accidental innuendo to genuine political analysis is funny and character-specific — these guys building an entire bipartisan cynicism theory on a butt joke. 'Coast-to-coast, nationwide ass blast' is a great escalation punchline.

jokes.text: Dee: 'No more! You guys are such morons. If you knew anything at all about politics, you would know that that is not true.'
jokes.setup: Dee positions herself as the informed adult in the room
jokes.punchline: Her correction leads directly to her pitching a bribe scheme, revealing her politics knowledge is just as self-serving and corrupt
jokes.explanation: Setup joke that earns its laugh retroactively when the 'correct' political knowledge turns out to be bribery. Works as ironic framing more than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: 'You have to be a real low-life piece of shit to get involved in politics' — cut to [02:10] where the gang is immediately plotting to run for office
jokes.setup: Dennis delivers a cynical verdict: only a lowlife piece of shit would get into politics
jokes.punchline: Scene cut to them already organizing the campaign, fully embodying exactly what Dennis described
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP structural joke — a character articulates the moral lesson and then immediately violates it. The scene cut IS the punchline. Perfect economy (the edit does all the work), strong character integration (the gang has zero self-awareness), and the structure is immaculate. This is the show's comedic identity in one edit.

jokes.text: 'What's the position?' / 'South Philly, Zone 2, District 37 Comptroller.' / 'Nice. What's a comptroller?' / 'Who gives a shit? We're doin' it for the bribe.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks what position they're running for; Frank reads the full official title
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks what a comptroller is; Frank dismisses the question entirely because they only care about the bribe
jokes.explanation: Very efficient joke. The 'Nice' reaction to an obscure bureaucratic position, followed by the admission they don't even know what it is, capped by 'Who gives a shit? We're doin' it for the bribe' is tight and characterful. Frank's bluntness is perfectly deployed.

jokes.text: 'Take a look at that hair... Kennedy hair. Note the bone structure. It's like a young J.F.K.'
jokes.setup: They need to pick who runs for office
jokes.punchline: The criteria is 'Kennedy hair' and bone structure — shallow, looks-based political reasoning that Dennis immediately buys into
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Dennis's vanity is flattered by the JFK comparison and he accepts the nomination instantly. The shallowness of their political calculus (it's literally just about hair) is a sharp satirical jab.

jokes.text: Mac makes a dismissive noise/face at the suggestion Dee has the same bone structure. Someone says 'Five head.' Dee protests she doesn't have that.
jokes.setup: Dee claims she has the same bone structure as Dennis (and JFK)
jokes.punchline: Mac's audible dismissal and the 'five head' insult — implying Dee's forehead is so large it's a 'five-head' instead of a forehead
jokes.explanation: 'Five head' is a solid wordplay insult — a known slang term deployed perfectly in context. Dee's incredulous denial ('I don't have that') is a good reaction beat. Part of the show's ongoing Dee-abuse comedy.

jokes.text: 'Deandra, a woman in politics is like a donkey doing calculus.'
jokes.setup: Dee wants to be involved in the campaign
jokes.punchline: Frank's simile is so casually, absurdly misogynistic — a donkey doing calculus — that it functions as both a character joke about Frank and a satirical exaggeration of political sexism
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The simile is structurally elegant — the absurdity of 'donkey doing calculus' (not a dumb animal, but specifically a non-math animal doing advanced math) makes it funnier than a straight insult. It's deeply Frank-specific — no other character delivers this. Highly quotable. Earns its dark-subversive tag because the show uses Frank's casual sexism as satire, not endorsement.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Come on. There are plenty of amazing women politicians. Name one.' Mac: 'Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton.' Mac: 'Awful.' Dee: 'How is she awful?' Mac: 'Hates freedom.'
jokes.setup: Dee challenges them to name an amazing woman politician
jokes.punchline: Mac names one, then immediately calls her 'awful' — and when pressed, the entire reasoning is 'hates freedom,' the most reductive political critique imaginable
jokes.explanation: Structurally very tight. The setup-subvert-subvert-again structure (name one → names one → she's awful → why? → hates freedom) is efficient comedy writing. 'Hates freedom' as the totality of political analysis is a sharp parody of lazy political discourse. Mac-specific voice.

jokes.text: Mac declares himself campaign manager because 'It's too late. I already have the clipboard.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Mac both want to be campaign manager
jokes.punchline: Mac's claim to authority is possession of a clipboard — as if holding a clipboard is legal proof of a job
jokes.explanation: Funny and sets up the clipboard as a running gag/power object throughout the episode. The clipboard becomes a totem of authority for these idiots. Good economy — 'I already have the clipboard' is all you need to get the joke.

jokes.text: They assign Charlie the role of intern. 'What does an intern do?' 'Cut limes.' 'Stock glasses.' 'Serve drinks.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is promised a role in the campaign as 'intern'
jokes.punchline: The intern duties are literally just bar work — cutting limes, stocking glasses — which is what Charlie already does. The 'campaign' is just the bar with a new title.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about how the gang's 'politics' never actually transcends their bar. Charlie's perpetual low-man status is reinforced — he's been given a fancy title for the same grunt work. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Frank enters and announces he will be campaign manager. Mac resists: 'You are way too old. Politics is a young man's game.'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to manage the campaign; Mac calls him too old
jokes.punchline: Mac declaring 'politics is a young man's game' — from a guy whose entire qualification is clipboard ownership — while Frank, a corrupt businessman, is objectively more qualified for political corruption than any of them
jokes.explanation: Decent setup for the upcoming vote joke. The irony of Mac being dismissive of someone more qualified is mild but functional.

jokes.text: Mac is immediately voted out as campaign manager by a show of hands. 'The people have spoken. You're out.' Mac: 'So that's it? I'm fired? This is bullshit!' Dennis: 'That's politics, man.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to consolidate power as campaign manager
jokes.punchline: He's immediately outvoted and fired from the job he just claimed; 'That's politics, man' becomes a recurring dismissal line
jokes.explanation: 'That's politics, man' is established here as a phrase that will recur throughout the episode. Mac's humiliation is swift and total — he went from power-grab to fired in under 60 seconds. Good comic rhythm. The rewatch bonus is for catching how 'that's politics' becomes a refrain.

jokes.text: Mac's storming out speech: 'This is bullshit! That's politics? That's politics? This is wonderful. I'm walkin' outta here. I don't need this shit. I'm washin' my hands of the whole situation. Show you, bitches.' Then: 'Can I grab that clipboard?' / 'No. That's mine.'
jokes.setup: Mac delivers an indignant exit speech
jokes.punchline: His entire dramatic exit is punctured by his attempt to take the clipboard — the one object of power — and being denied even that
jokes.explanation: The clipboard callback deflates Mac's dramatic exit perfectly. He can't even execute a dignified storming-out without reaching for the clipboard. The bathos is well-timed and the structure is clean — big speech, small humiliation.

jokes.text: Charlie shows Dennis his blazer. 'Yeah. It's too small.' / 'Nah. It's perfect.'
jokes.setup: Charlie asked if he should wear a blazer for the campaign
jokes.punchline: He shows up in a blazer that's visibly too small — and genuinely believes it looks perfect
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that works on character — Charlie is oblivious to how he looks. The blazer is too small and he thinks it's perfect. Simple but effective. Gets funnier when Frank later calls it out more harshly.

jokes.text: Dee reports: 'Full of hoboes, Dennis. A lot of hoboes.' Dennis and Charlie look around at the bar.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks how the bar is doing
jokes.punchline: The bar is currently full of hoboes — the first hint of Frank's 'hobo-vertising' scheme
jokes.explanation: Good economy — 'Full of hoboes, Dennis. A lot of hoboes.' is a great deadpan line. Sets up the hobo-vertising reveal efficiently.

jokes.text: Frank reveals his campaign strategy: 'Hobo-vertising' — putting campaign signs on actual hoboes
jokes.setup: Frank has been filling the bar with hoboes; Charlie is concerned about the campaign's image
jokes.punchline: 'Hobo-vertising' — using homeless people as human billboards, delivered with complete sincerity and pride
jokes.explanation: 'Hobo-vertising' is a genuinely great IASIP-style compound word — it's dark (exploiting homeless people), absurd (as a sincere campaign strategy), and completely Frank-specific. The portmanteau is well-coined and immediately memorable. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted. Frank's pride in the concept makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Charlie to Dennis: 'Hobo-vertising? That's not you. It's cheap. It's cheap politics. It's not gonna get us that bribe.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is objecting to hobo-vertising on the grounds of campaign image
jokes.punchline: Charlie's concern is not ethical — it's purely strategic: cheap tactics won't get them the bribe money they're after
jokes.explanation: Good IASIP irony — Charlie sounds like a principled campaign advisor for half a sentence before revealing his actual concern is bribery optics. The moral vacuum is funny and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Charlie campaign manager pitch: 'I mean, when I look at you, I see success. I see... You're top-notch. You're goin' all the way with this thing.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to convince Dennis to make him campaign manager by flattering him
jokes.punchline: His pitch is painfully empty — pure meaningless flattery with no substance, delivered with desperate sincerity
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny cringe — Charlie's desperation and emptiness of the pitch is characterful but not particularly sharp writing.

jokes.text: Dennis talking head/confessional: 'I just didn't realize I was gonna have to make so many... tough decisions.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been making petty, ridiculous decisions about who holds a clipboard
jokes.punchline: He frames firing Frank and Mac from a fake campaign as 'so many tough decisions' — treating trivial nonsense with gravitas
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP talking-head humor. Dennis's self-importance inflating minor chaos into presidential-weight decisions is pitch-perfect character comedy. The pause before 'tough decisions' sells it.

jokes.text: Frank is being taken down off a hobo by Dennis and Charlie. Frank: 'This is a goddamn coup!'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are removing Frank's hobo-vertising operation — literally taking signs off hoboes
jokes.punchline: Frank screams 'This is a goddamn coup!' as if he's being politically overthrown rather than having sandwich-boards removed from homeless men
jokes.explanation: Good visual-physical comedy moment. Frank's escalated language ('coup') against the mundane reality of the situation is very funny. The image of grown men physically dismantling 'hobo-vertising' is inherently absurd.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Don't take it personally, Dad. That's just politics.' Frank: 'You look like a dick in that tiny jacket.'
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses Frank with the now-established 'that's politics' line
jokes.punchline: Frank retaliates by going after Charlie's too-small blazer — confirming it does look bad — which everyone then tries to protect
jokes.explanation: Double callback — to the blazer visual gag and the 'that's politics' refrain. Frank's 'you look like a dick in that tiny jacket' is a great insult, and everyone defending the jacket ('Don't go after the jacket') makes it funnier. Well-executed callback structure.

jokes.text: The clipboard tug-of-war: Frank demands it, Charlie refuses, they physically struggle over it as the symbol of power
jokes.setup: Frank wants the clipboard as symbol of authority
jokes.punchline: Adults physically fighting over a clipboard as if it confers real power
jokes.explanation: The clipboard-as-power-object running gag pays off here with physical comedy. The escalation from Mac claiming it to Frank and Charlie fighting over it is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Dennis's reaction after the clipboard fight: 'Wow. That was, uh, a lot easier than I thought it was gonna be.'
jokes.setup: An absurd multi-party fight over a clipboard just occurred
jokes.punchline: Dennis's breezy, detached assessment that it was 'a lot easier than I thought' — treating the chaos as routine
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan reaction beat. Dennis's sociopathic calm in the wake of manufactured chaos is a character staple. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Mac to Dee: 'We're gonna stroll right into that comptroller's office and solicit a bribe.' Mac reveals his bribe plan.
jokes.setup: Mac was fired from the campaign for being incompetent
jokes.punchline: His counter-move is to run a parallel competing bribe scheme — he's going to out-corrupt his own side
jokes.explanation: Functional plot/comedy beat. The fact that the fired campaign manager immediately starts his own competing bribe operation is a good absurdist escalation of the premise.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Now let's get you ready for the ball, Cinderella.' He proceeds to try to manage Dee's appearance while she is visibly uncomfortable.
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to make Dee look like a viable political candidate
jokes.punchline: He calls her Cinderella with zero irony, then immediately starts fixing her 'bangs' and referencing her 'five head' — the makeover is an extended insult
jokes.explanation: Cringe-comfortable Dee abuse. The 'Cinderella' framing followed by immediate insult-as-compliment is decent. The five-head callback is noted.

jokes.text: Mac to union guys: 'You know, like, in the movies, union guys are, like, tough and shady and shit.' The union guys are visibly nerdy and straight-laced.
jokes.setup: Mac expects movie-style tough union guys to help him run a bribe scheme
jokes.punchline: The actual union guys are mild-mannered bureaucrats — the gap between Mac's expectation and reality is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good subverted expectation. Mac's pop-culture-shaped worldview (he thinks he's in a movie) crashing against reality is a solid IASIP beat. Sets up the 'nerd' insult that drives Act Two.

jokes.text: Mac's 'let me take you bitches to school' speech about how 'in this country, in the real world, people make money' — delivered as if it's profound wisdom
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to pitch corruption to two straight-laced union officials
jokes.punchline: His 'wisdom' is essentially just 'money exists' — delivered with intense confidence as if he's revealing secrets of the universe
jokes.explanation: Mac's bravado over empty content is a consistent character beat. 'Let me take you bitches to school' as the intro to 'people make money' is a good deflation.

jokes.text: Mac becomes convinced the meeting is bugged by the feds, starts speaking in elaborate conspiracy code — 'We are not a criminal organization. No, sir.' — while dramatically looking around
jokes.setup: Union guy says clearly 'we are not a criminal organization'
jokes.punchline: Mac interprets the totally straightforward statement as elaborate FBI-evasion code, starts playing along by saying the same things, completely misreading the situation
jokes.explanation: Good sustained absurdist character bit. Mac's movie-brain interpreting mundane straight talk as coded mob speak is very funny. 'I read. I see movies. I understand.' is a perfect character line — he's learned about the world exclusively through pop culture. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Mac's exit from the union meeting: 'Okay, gentlemen, sorry we couldn't work anything out. But, uh, I'm gonna go home and pay my taxes. Right?' — massive wink energy
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to exit while maintaining his 'we're not criminals' cover
jokes.punchline: His cover story — 'going home to pay taxes' — is so transparently fake it's the loudest possible signal that he's a criminal
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the anti-surveillance bit. The 'going home to pay my taxes' exit line is a nice touch of absurd non-cover story.

jokes.text: Union guy to his partner after Mac leaves: 'I've got a better idea. Let's screw this son of a bitch.' Partner: 'Come on, Morris. We don't have time for this.' Morris: 'He called us nerds, Gary.' [pause] 'Nerds.'
jokes.setup: Mac insulted the union guys by calling them nerds — clearly not intending to weaponize the insult
jokes.punchline: The union guys decide to run a full criminal sting operation on Mac — not for money, not for power — but purely because he called them nerds. 'Nerds.' delivered as the final solemn justification.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The pivot to the union guys having their own character-driven motivation — wounded pride over being called nerds — is a genuinely surprising and delightful twist. 'Nerds.' as the single-word final beat, delivered with gravitas over a cut to black, is perfect timing and economy. The joke subverts the expectation that only the gang are petty and irrational — the 'straight men' are equally petty. The pause and repetition are masterfully written.

jokes.text: Dennis's campaign response to crime: 'I say we put 'em on busses, ship 'em over to Iraq... make 'em fight the terrorists.'
jokes.setup: Voter asks Dennis about the crime problem
jokes.punchline: His policy is to deport criminals to a war zone as a fighting force — an utterly insane but confidently delivered position
jokes.explanation: Dark and absurd policy proposal delivered with complete sincerity. The voter responds with 'You're very handsome' — suggesting she was charmed despite the insane policy. Good satirical edge.

jokes.text: Voter: 'You're very handsome.' Dennis: 'Thank you.' Charlie: 'They love the bone structure.'
jokes.setup: Dennis just proposed a genuinely insane crime policy
jokes.punchline: The voter responds to his looks, not his policy — confirming the gang's (horrible) theory that politics is about appearance. Charlie's 'they love the bone structure' is a perfect callback.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical payoff — their shallow theory about politics (it's all looks) is validated in the most damning way possible. The voter ignores a terrible policy and compliments his face. 'They love the bone structure' is well-timed and quotable.

jokes.text: Mac returns, wanting back in. Dennis: 'First you wash your hands of politics. Now you want back in. That's called flip-flopping. That's what Democrats do.'
jokes.setup: Mac stormed out saying he was done; now he's back wanting in
jokes.punchline: Dennis accuses him of 'flip-flopping... that's what Democrats do' — using real political rhetoric in a completely petty, absurd context
jokes.explanation: Good political satire micro-joke. Using 'flip-flopping' (a 2000s political buzzword) to describe someone changing their mind about a fake bribe campaign in a bar is funny.

jokes.text: Mac tries to kiss a baby for the campaign. His baby-kissing pitch escalates from polite request to 'Goddamn it! Just give me the baby!' as the mother screams for help.
jokes.setup: Mac's re-entry scheme is to do traditional campaign baby-kissing
jokes.punchline: He cannot execute even the most basic political gesture without it becoming a terrifying confrontation — screaming at a mother to give him her baby in public
jokes.explanation: Very good escalation sequence. Mac starts professionally ('I couldn't help but notice your adorable baby') and within 30 seconds is screaming 'Goddamn it! Just give me the baby!' The escalation is well-paced and character-consistent — Mac's social incompetence and impatience are perfectly expressed. 'This is campaign suicide, dude' as the kicker works.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'This is campaign suicide, dude.' — after Mac screams at the mother
jokes.setup: Mac's baby incident causes the mother to scream for help
jokes.punchline: Dennis's calm political analysis of the optics while they flee is comically detached
jokes.explanation: Button on the baby scene. Dennis's concern is purely electoral, not ethical — he's not worried about Mac terrorizing a mother, he's worried about the optics. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Frank is trying to make Dee look sexy for the political meeting. 'I think I look like a whore.' Frank: 'I'm trying to make you sexy.'
jokes.setup: Frank is prepping Dee as a political 'threat' to the opponent
jokes.punchline: Dee's entirely accurate self-assessment ('I look like a whore') is dismissed by Frank who treats 'sexy' and 'whore' as different categories while his styling suggests otherwise
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe setup. Frank's oblivious makeover destroying Dee's dignity is on-brand. Functions more as setup for the extended 'Dee as political asset' joke.

jokes.text: Dee: 'There is nothing more threatening to a man than a woman who is smart and attractive.' Frank: 'We have to pretend you're both.'
jokes.setup: Someone (Mac or Frank) gives the inspirational line about smart and attractive women being threatening
jokes.punchline: 'We have to pretend you're both' — delivered to Dee's face, implying she is neither smart nor attractive
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The structure is a textbook misdirect: the inspirational setup ('nothing more threatening than a smart, attractive woman') is completely subverted by the reveal that the person saying it doesn't believe Dee qualifies. The timing and economy are excellent — 'pretend you're both' does enormous damage in four words. Highly quotable, strong character integration (Frank's casual cruelty to Dee).

jokes.text: Dee: 'Wow. You're a horrible father.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just told his daughter they need to pretend she's smart and attractive
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat, matter-of-fact assessment: 'You're a horrible father' — no anger, just tired acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: Good button on the previous joke. Dee's weary understatement is funnier than outrage would be. The relationship between Frank and Dee is well-characterized in five words.

jokes.text: Mac's inner monologue/mutter while alone: 'Oh, don't hurt my baby. Like I'm gonna hurt somebody's baby. You know what I mean? Goddamn Dennis. Fire me? I'll fire you.'
jokes.setup: Mac is alone, apparently walking somewhere, still stewing about being fired
jokes.punchline: He's still relitigating the baby incident and the firing simultaneously, in a private muttered rant, talking to himself
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Mac can't let anything go and processes grievances through muttering. The parallel grievances (baby and job) running simultaneously is characterful.

jokes.text: Union guy in car: 'We got a bribe for your roommate's withdrawal from the race.' Mac is visibly surprised. 'Really? Wow. You nerds work fast.'
jokes.setup: Mac insulted the union guys as nerds; they've now organized a whole sting operation
jokes.punchline: Mac calls them nerds AGAIN to their faces — the very insult that set all this in motion — while complimenting their efficiency
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic callback. Mac is literally repeating the insult that caused the problem while thinking he's giving a compliment. The audience knows something Mac doesn't. Well-structured dramatic irony that lands.

jokes.text: Union guy's henchman: 'Otherwise, Marvin here is gonna have to take care of you.' Mac: 'Take care of me how?' Marvin: 'I'll probably stab you in your throat.'
jokes.setup: The union guys are threatening Mac with their enforcer 'taking care' of him — standard mob-movie language
jokes.punchline: Instead of a vague threat, Marvin provides a hyperspecific, clinical answer: 'I'll probably stab you in your throat'
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The setup uses the conventional 'take care of you' gangster euphemism, then subverts it by having Marvin provide an extremely specific and casual answer: 'I'll probably stab you in your throat.' The word 'probably' is what makes it funny — the casual uncertainty about the method of violence. Highly quotable. Mac's 'Jesus Christ! Stab me in my throat?' reaction sells it.

jokes.text: Mac is visibly terrified and quickly agrees. 'I'm gonna pull him out. I'm gonna pull him out, Marvin. Marvin, I'm gonna pull him out.' Then, as the car drives away: 'Who's the nerd now, bitch?'
jokes.setup: Mac has just been threatened with throat-stabbing and immediately capitulated
jokes.punchline: He reasserts dominance to the departed car with 'Who's the nerd now, bitch?' — having just completely caved to them
jokes.explanation: Great character beat. Mac's bravado reasserts the second the threat is gone — he was completely subservient while in danger, then immediately claims victory as the car drives away. 'Who's the nerd now, bitch?' is quotable and character-perfect. His cowardice masked by delayed bravado is a core Mac trait.

jokes.text: Union guy Gary (under his breath): 'That was fun. I feel like a gangster.' Morris: 'Shut up, Gary.'
jokes.setup: Morris ran a whole intimidation operation; Gary enjoyed it too much
jokes.punchline: Gary's wide-eyed admission that he feels like a gangster undercuts the whole intimidating scene; Morris's tired 'Shut up, Gary' is a perfect straight-man button
jokes.explanation: Fantastic button joke on the whole union sequence. Gary's admission humanizes these ostensible antagonists and deflates the tension perfectly. 'Shut up, Gary' is an ideal two-word punchline. The reveal that the 'nerd' union guys were secretly thrilled to do something cool is a perfect mirror to Mac's earlier posturing. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Mac to Dennis: 'I didn't wanna say this before, but you don't have Kennedy hair.' / Dennis: 'All right! Oh, God!'
jokes.setup: Mac now needs Dennis to drop out of the race; earlier he built Dennis up with the Kennedy hair claim
jokes.punchline: He now weaponizes the same compliment as an insult — 'you don't have Kennedy hair' — the second he needs leverage. Dennis's devastated reaction suggests he fully believed it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The Kennedy hair compliment, used to recruit Dennis, is now used as a weapon to destroy his confidence. Dennis's outsized reaction ('All right! Oh, God!') is perfect — he cares about the Kennedy hair comparison deeply. Character-specific and structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: Frank holds up what he describes as 'a million-dollar bill pal' as a campaign prop — a fake million-dollar bill
jokes.setup: Campaign commercial shoot in Paddy's bar
jokes.punchline: Frank's prop for the commercial is a fake million-dollar bill — a novelty item presented as serious campaign imagery
jokes.explanation: Minor absurdist gag — a million-dollar bill doesn't exist, used as a campaign prop in a basement commercial. Part of the general incompetence comedy.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'It's not about the bribe anymore. I could be a legitimate politician. Really do some good in Philadelphia.' Everyone reacts with incredulity. 'You've never done any good for anybody ever!' / 'I do good!'
jokes.setup: Dennis has become genuinely caught up in the campaign fantasy
jokes.punchline: His pivot to 'doing good' is met with immediate and total disbelief from everyone who actually knows him — and his defense ('I do good! I do good!') is pathetically unconvincing
jokes.explanation: Good character-based comedy. Dennis's delusional self-image (a person who does good) crashing against the reality everyone else sees is classic IASIP. 'You've never done any good for anybody ever!' is a great character-specific attack.

jokes.text: Charlie locks Dennis in the bar to prevent him from dropping out. Dennis: 'You are going to hell, little man!' Charlie: 'Mmm, I don't think so. That's politics, bitch.'
jokes.setup: Charlie needs Dennis to stay in the race; Dennis is about to leave
jokes.punchline: Charlie uses Dennis's own dismissal phrase — 'That's politics' — against him while literally imprisoning him in a bar
jokes.explanation: Great callback payoff for 'that's politics.' The phrase has been used by multiple characters to dismiss people; Charlie weaponizing it while locking Dennis in a bar is a great structural callback. 'That's politics, bitch' as an addition to the established phrase is a small but good escalation.

jokes.text: Dennis asks: 'Dude, you and my dad share this futon?' Charlie: 'No. No, we... No, we got a whole different situation worked out.' [awkward pause]
jokes.setup: Dennis notices the living situation while locked in Charlie/Frank's apartment
jokes.punchline: Charlie's attempt to explain the sleeping arrangement collapses into incoherence — 'I sleep on the... And...' — suggesting the situation is too strange or shameful to articulate
jokes.explanation: Good IASIP dark-subtext joke. The implication that Frank and Charlie's living arrangement is something Charlie can barely articulate ('the whole different situation') is funny and disturbing. The stammering non-answer is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Charlie's campaign script: 'Hello, fellow American. This you should vote me. I leave power. Good. Thank you. Thank you. If you vote me, I am hot.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has written a campaign speech for Dennis to deliver on camera
jokes.punchline: The script is complete grammatical chaos — 'This you should vote me' / 'I am hot' — suggesting Charlie either can't write English properly or is functionally illiterate
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a cornerstone of Charlie's character — his illiteracy/dyslexia is established here as a running character trait. The script is phenomenally written bad writing: each line sounds like a different kind of wrong ('This you should vote me' is Yoda-syntax; 'I am hot' is a non-sequitur policy statement). The specificity of the bad writing makes it funnier than generic gibberish. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, strong rewatch value as a touchstone Charlie moment.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'This doesn't make any sense.' Charlie: 'Well, then just say whatever you want.' Then: 'The battery's dead. It's gone.'
jokes.setup: After Charlie's script is rejected as nonsensical, Dennis is told to improvise
jokes.punchline: Before he can say a single word of improvised speech, the camera battery dies — the entire effort was pointless
jokes.explanation: Perfect punctuation joke on the whole ad sequence. The elaborate failed preparation (the script, the blazer, the beach-towel backdrop, the tanning reflector) ends before anything is recorded. The anti-climax is the punchline. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Frank touching Dee: 'This one piece is makin' me nervous.' Dee: 'You seriously need to stop touching me. This is really ridiculous. I'm stuffed in here like a jerk.'
jokes.setup: Frank is still futzing with Dee's outfit before the meeting
jokes.punchline: Dee's mounting frustration ('I'm stuffed in here like a jerk') is a great image — suggesting Frank has crammed her into something uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe beat. 'I'm stuffed in here like a jerk' is a funny Dee-specific complaint. Mildly amusing filler before the Stanford scene.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Deandra, you look sensational.' Dee: 'No, I don't.'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to build Dee up before the meeting
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat 'No, I don't' — she has zero faith in Frank's styling or his honesty at this point
jokes.explanation: Quick and efficient. The lack of any enthusiasm in Dee's 'No, I don't' is funny in its resignation. Good economy.

jokes.text: Frank to Dee: 'Just remember. Let Daddy do all the talkin'.'
jokes.setup: Frank has dressed Dee up as bait and is about to use her as a prop to solicit a bribe
jokes.punchline: 'Let Daddy do all the talkin'' — Frank deploying his daughter as a prop while calling himself 'Daddy' in this context is deeply creepy in a way the show plays for laughs
jokes.explanation: Dark subversive Frank moment — the 'Daddy' framing while literally pimping out his daughter for political corruption is on-brand dark IASIP. Funny and disturbing in the right ratio.

jokes.text: Frank to Stanford: 'Check out the goods to my right. This pretty little lady is not only my daughter. She happens to be your biggest opponent in the election. Beauty and the beast.'
jokes.setup: Frank is presenting Dee as a political threat to Stanford
jokes.punchline: 'Beauty and the beast' — Frank seemingly compliments the situation but the ambiguity of who is the beast (Dee? Stanford?) makes it funnier; either way Frank is insulting his own daughter
jokes.explanation: Good wordplay — 'beauty and the beast' is ambiguous about which is which, and given Frank's established view of Dee's attractiveness, it's likely he means Dee is the beast. The casualness with which Frank says this is characterful.

jokes.text: Stanford's response to the bribe attempt: 'Are you trying to solicit a bribe from me? ... not only is that illegal and highly unethical, but you're doing it with the subtlety of a baboon.'
jokes.setup: Frank has made the most clumsy, obvious bribe pitch imaginable
jokes.punchline: Stanford's response acknowledges the illegality but his real objection is the craftwork: 'you're doing it with the subtlety of a baboon' — an objection to the quality of the crime, not the crime itself
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. The structure of the objection — illegal AND unethical AND badly executed — with the kicker being the baboon simile, is very well written. 'Subtlety of a baboon' is a great quotable insult. The implication that he might have been open to a better-executed bribe is a sharp satirical note.

jokes.text: Stanford invites Dee to dinner. Frank interrupts: 'My little girl don't go nowhere without her old man.' Dee, dead-eyed: 'You're fired.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been micromanaging Dee; Stanford tries to cut him out by inviting Dee directly
jokes.punchline: Dee fires Frank on the spot, with zero hesitation — having waited for the first opportunity to do so
jokes.explanation: Good payoff. Dee's decisive firing of Frank echoes the episode's firing motif. The speed with which she says it — no buildup, just 'You're fired' — is the joke. Frank getting cut out by his own prop is satisfying structurally.

jokes.text: Mac's smear tape narration: 'Dennis Reynolds was sent home for the statutory rape of a teenage camper. / A vote for Dennis Reynolds is a vote for underage rape. / Dennis Reynolds... baby rapist. / Don't let him rape you, Philadelphia.'
jokes.setup: Mac has obtained a tape of a Dennis scandal from camp
jokes.punchline: The narration escalates from 'statutory rape' to 'baby rapist' to the direct-address 'Don't let him rape you, Philadelphia' — each title more extreme and absurd than the last
jokes.explanation: Very strong dark comedy escalation. The progression from legal terminology to 'baby rapist' to the PSA-style 'Don't let him rape you, Philadelphia' is a perfect three-step escalation. Each title is more insane. The direct address to Philadelphia as a potential rape victim is the peak absurdity. Quotable, dark, well-paced.

jokes.text: Dennis's response to being called a 'baby rapist': 'You raped a girl?' Dennis: 'No, no. Okay. Rape? I was accused of... Okay, statutory, first of all. Not... I kissed her. She was a year younger than me. That's not... even statutory or anything.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is confronted with Mac's smear tape calling him a 'baby rapist'
jokes.punchline: Dennis's defense is a scrambled series of legal distinctions that collapse into 'I kissed her. She was a year younger than me.' — a defense that actually raises more questions
jokes.explanation: Good character cringe. Dennis's flustered non-denial ('Okay, statutory, first of all. Not... I kissed her.') reads as incriminating rather than exculpatory. The fact that he's making these distinctions at all is damning. Character-specific to Dennis's dark side.

jokes.text: Charlie reads Frank's note: 'All right. Yeah. All right. Uh, 'Meet'... Starts out 'Meet,' and then there's, like, other stuff.' Dennis: 'You clearly have a learning disability, dude.'
jokes.setup: Frank has left a note for Mac to meet him
jokes.punchline: Charlie can't read it properly — 'starts out Meet and then there's like other stuff' — confirming the dyslexia/illiteracy established with his script
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Charlie's reading/writing problems. 'Starts out Meet and then there's like other stuff' as a description of a note is perfectly Charlie. Dennis's 'you clearly have a learning disability' is a great straight-man line. Reinforces the character through plot action.

jokes.text: Mac arrives at the parking garage in a trench coat. Frank: 'Where'd you get that trench coat?' Mac: 'It's cool, huh?' Frank: 'It's very cool. That was a smart buy.'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives for a secret parking garage meeting
jokes.punchline: The meeting is immediately derailed by both of them admiring Mac's trench coat — conspiratorial business takes a back seat to fashion appreciation
jokes.explanation: Good IASIP joke — the clandestine spy-movie meeting is immediately humanized/deflated by both conspirators stopping to compliment a coat. Character-specific to both Mac's vanity and Frank's chaotic sincerity.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I'm gonna need you to beg.' Mac: 'Don't make me beg.' Frank: 'You gotta beg.' Mac: 'Seriously?' Frank: 'Seriously. Down. Down.'
jokes.setup: Frank has the smear tape and Mac wants it
jokes.punchline: Frank refuses to negotiate — his price is public humiliation. Mac has to literally get down and beg.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-power dynamic. Frank using this as an opportunity to humiliate Mac is characterful. The begging sequence is an escalating degradation that works well.

jokes.text: Frank reveals he gave the tape to Charlie, who traded it for the Garbage Pail Kids. Mac: 'Oh, my God. This is bad. This is so bad, man.' Frank: 'These things, Mac... You don't know how rare they are. These are rare. You can't find these.'
jokes.setup: Mac was about to get the tape through begging; Frank reveals Charlie already traded for it using the 'investment'
jokes.punchline: Frank's response to this political crisis is to wax rhapsodic about the rarity of Garbage Pail Kids — the entire opening scene's investment framing has now paid off absurdly
jokes.explanation: Excellent long-form callback payoff. Charlie's Garbage Pail Kids being treated as an investment in the opening scene now pays off — he traded his entire 'retirement plan' for the tape, and Frank validates the investment framing by admiring the cards' rarity. The irony is that the 'investment' was wasted on a political crisis that immediately collapses. Structurally very satisfying.

jokes.text: Frank to Mac, with zero sympathy: 'That is politics, bitch.'
jokes.setup: Mac is in serious trouble over the bribe scheme and needed the tape
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses him with the episode's signature phrase — 'That is politics, bitch' — the ultimate deployment of the running gag
jokes.explanation: Running gag culmination. Frank adding 'bitch' to the established phrase and deploying it at a moment of genuine crisis elevates it slightly. Good running gag execution.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I am in some serious shit. I needed him to drop out.' Frank: 'I don't care what you need. That is politics, bitch.'
jokes.setup: Mac explains he needed the tape to make Dennis drop out
jokes.punchline: Frank deploys 'That is politics, bitch' — the fourth use of the episode's catchphrase, now used by Frank to dismiss Mac's crisis
jokes.explanation: Fourth deployment of the catchphrase — now it's fully infected everyone in the gang. The phrase has migrated from Charlie to Dennis to Charlie again to now Frank, each time used as a smug justification for self-interest. Good running gag management.

jokes.text: Stanford's wife appears at the bar: 'Who's the slut?' Stanford: 'Honey, this isn't what...' Wife: 'Another one of your whores? Who do you think you are... Bill Clinton? You're a comptroller.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Stanford are having drinks; his wife walks in
jokes.punchline: 'Who do you think you are... Bill Clinton? You're a comptroller.' — The Clinton comparison is immediately deflated by the reminder that he's a glorified accountant. The gap between his self-image and reality is the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The Bill Clinton comparison is perfect — sexual scandal + political figure — but the kicker 'You're a comptroller' instantly deflates it. The joke captures the entire episode's satirical thesis: these people are playing at politics but they're just small-time nobodies. 'Bill Clinton? You're a comptroller.' is a highly quotable, beautifully structured line. The wife's character voice is perfect.

jokes.text: Stanford's wife: 'Who do you think you are... Bill Clinton? You're a comptroller.'
jokes.setup: Wife confronts cheating husband Stanford
jokes.punchline: She deflates his self-importance with 'You're a comptroller' — the job that the entire episode has been about, now used as the ultimate status diminishment
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback joke. The episode opened with Mac asking 'What's a comptroller?' — positioning it as an obscure, minor position. Now 'you're a comptroller' is used as the definitive put-down (you're no Clinton, you're just an accountant). The economy is superb — four words deflate both the man and the episode's entire political premise. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Mac returns to the bar having obtained 'the smear tape.' 'Oh, hey, man. That's great. Yes!' Then Dee walks in disheveled: 'Screw politicians.' Mac: 'No time for that. We gotta get back out on that campaign trail.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just had a terrible, humiliating experience with the married politician
jokes.punchline: Mac's complete obliviousness to Dee's distress — immediately trying to drag her back into the campaign — is characteristically self-centered
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat. Mac's obliviousness is on-brand. Mostly functional transition humor.

jokes.text: Dennis drops out: 'I googled "comptroller." Turns out that this guy's really just a glorified accountant... I hate doing math. It sounds like a ton of work... These guys make less than teachers.'
jokes.setup: Mac pushes Dennis to continue the campaign
jokes.punchline: Dennis's entire political aspiration evaporates the moment he discovers the job is real work with modest pay — the lazy narcissist's research
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis character moment. His entire political journey ends because Google revealed it involves math and pays less than teachers. The escalation of his reasoning ('I hate doing math' → 'it's a ton of work' → 'less than teachers') is excellent Dennis logic. His brief flirtation with legitimate public service is exactly as deep as his narcissism allows.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Oh, yeah. I googled "comptroller." Turns out that this guy's really just a glorified accountant. You know what I mean? And I hate doing math. It sounds like a ton of work. These guys, they make less than teachers.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been chasing the bribe and dreaming of political power
jokes.punchline: He googled the job. It's a glorified accountant. He hates math. He's out. His entire motivation collapses on the most basic due diligence.
jokes.explanation: Very good character-comedy. The entire episode's premise collapses because Dennis did 30 seconds of research that none of them thought to do earlier. 'They make less than teachers' as the clincher is perfect — it's not about corruption or morality, it's about the pay. Character-specific to Dennis's laziness and self-interest.

jokes.text: Charlie insists Dennis has to run. Dennis: 'No, I don't. You're not the boss of me.' Charlie: 'I'm the campaign manager.' Dennis: 'You're fired.' Charlie: 'I traded all my Garbage Pail Kids for you.' Dennis: 'Well, that was stupid.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is desperate for Dennis to stay in the race; Dennis quits anyway
jokes.punchline: Charlie's heartbreaking reveal that he traded his entire Garbage Pail Kids collection (his 'investment' / 'future') for the smear tape is met with Dennis's brutal 'Well, that was stupid.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. This is the culmination of the episode's longest-running gag — Charlie's Garbage Pail Kids were 'his future,' 'an investment,' items of genuine value to him. He traded them all away for the smear tape to help Dennis, who immediately quits and dismisses the sacrifice with 'Well, that was stupid.' The brutality of Dennis's response and the pathos of Charlie's loss combine into perfect IASIP dark comedy. Deeply character-specific, structurally satisfying as a long-form payoff, and 'Well, that was stupid' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Cut to: Dee alone, still in her 'sexy' outfit. Someone (Frank?) says: 'Bit of an overreaction, don't you think?' / 'You look like a whore.'
jokes.setup: Dee has presumably done something dramatic in response to her humiliation
jokes.punchline: 'You look like a whore' as a reaction to whatever Dee did — the insult is both a callback to her earlier self-assessment and a dismissal of whatever emotional response she just had
jokes.explanation: Callback to Dee's earlier whore self-assessment. Decent beat that reinforces Dee's humiliation throughout the episode.

jokes.text: Mac arrives for another secret meeting wearing Frank's trench coat: 'Is that Frank's trench coat?' Mac: 'Yeah. Pretty sweet, right?' Charlie: 'Totally sweet.'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives dramatically for a clandestine meeting
jokes.punchline: He's wearing Frank's trench coat — the same coat admired in the parking garage — now borrowed, and both characters pause to admire it again
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the trench coat gag. The two of them again prioritizing coat appreciation over their criminal conspiracy is consistent and funny.

jokes.text: Mac says he needs to 'make Dennis disappear.' Charlie's immediate reaction: 'Ah! Ah! That's what I'm talkin' about. / I was thinkin' that same thing, man.'
jokes.setup: Mac needs Dennis out of the race
jokes.punchline: Charlie's enthusiastic agreement suggests he immediately interprets 'make Dennis disappear' as murder — and is on board
jokes.explanation: Good dark subversive misdirect. Charlie's instant enthusiastic agreement with what he thinks is a murder plot is characterful. The reveal that he was going to suggest guns and piano wire ('If we use a gun, we're gonna need a silencer... Fine. No guns. Piano wire.') makes the joke land harder.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the plan is just taking Dennis to Atlantic City for a few days. 'Retard. I'm talking about taking Dennis to Atlantic City for a couple of days until the election is over.' Charlie: 'What are you talkin' about?'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been planning a murder operation
jokes.punchline: The 'make Dennis disappear' plan is just Atlantic City for a few days. The deflation of Charlie's murder preparation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the murder misdirection sequence. 'Retard. I'm talking about taking Dennis to Atlantic City' punctures all the dark escalation. Charlie's bewildered 'What are you talkin' about?' suggests he's genuinely confused that the murder plot is off the table. Well-structured misdirection payoff.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I give the guy my blood, sweat and tears, right? And my Garbage Pail Kids. And... And he just drops right out of the race on me.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is expressing his grievance over Dennis quitting
jokes.punchline: He lists 'my blood, sweat and tears' and 'my Garbage Pail Kids' as equivalent sacrifices — the Garbage Pail Kids as a solemn offering alongside his literal human effort
jokes.explanation: Late-episode callback that still lands. The juxtaposition of 'blood, sweat and tears' with 'my Garbage Pail Kids' placed as a solemn afterthought is a great beat. Charlie's genuine emotional investment in both is a character-specific detail that keeps giving.

jokes.text: 'As long as we hurt him a little bit...' Charlie mutters as Mac walks away.
jokes.setup: Mac has called off the Atlantic City plan too; Charlie is left with nothing
jokes.punchline: Charlie's parting wish — 'as long as we hurt him a little bit' — reveals that murder being off the table doesn't mean he's let go of violence entirely
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark button on the whole Atlantic City/murder sequence. Charlie's small petulant wish for a little bit of violence — after all his elaborate murder planning — is a great character note. Economy is excellent; the line is thrown away but lands.

jokes.text: Mac starts to run away. 'Looks like you bitches shouldn't have fired me in the first place. Are you kiddin' me? Are you kiddin' me with that? I'm gonna buy myself a car. I am gonna drive as far away from this goddamn city—'
jokes.setup: Mac thinks he's about to collect the bribe money and escape
jokes.punchline: He starts his triumphant escape speech — but we can tell from the edit he's about to be caught
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for the police sting. Mac's triumphalist speech before being immediately arrested is a classic hubris-deflation structure. Decent execution.

jokes.text: Police officers confront Mac. 'Conspiracy to solicit a bribe. Racketeering. I'd say there's a big problem.' 'Your buddy over at the union came to see us recently.' 'Apparently, you called him a nerd, Mac.'
jokes.setup: Mac is arrested; the cops explain why
jokes.punchline: The cops list serious federal crimes — conspiracy, racketeering — and then add: 'Apparently, you called him a nerd, Mac.' The nerd insult is cited by police as the apparent motive for the sting.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The 'nerd' insult that started as an offhand slight has resulted in Mac facing federal racketeering charges. The police officer saying 'Apparently, you called him a nerd, Mac' as part of a list of serious crimes is a perfect structural joke — the small pettiness (name-calling) has escalated to enormous consequences. This is the episode's thematic punchline about petty vengeance and political corruption operating at the same level.

jokes.text: Police: 'You're goin' away for a long time... and prison can be a very unpleasant place for a good-lookin' young man like yourself.' Other cop: 'Oh, yeah. They're gonna tear through you like Kleenex.'
jokes.setup: Police are threatening Mac with prison as leverage
jokes.punchline: 'They're gonna tear through you like Kleenex' — an extremely specific and graphic prison rape metaphor delivered matter-of-factly by a police officer
jokes.explanation: Dark and very specific. 'Tear through you like Kleenex' as a prison threat is both vivid and oddly poetic. The casualness of the delivery by a police officer makes it funnier and darker simultaneously. The simile is memorable and quotable.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Are you soliciting a bribe from me?' Police officer: 'Sorry, pal. That's politics.'
jokes.setup: The cops want something to make Mac's arrest go away — implying they want a bribe
jokes.punchline: Mac recognizes the structure: 'Are you soliciting a bribe from me?' The cop closes the entire episode with 'Sorry, pal. That's politics.' — the episode's signature phrase deployed in its final form, as the actual final line
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and the perfect closing joke. The structure is immaculate: Mac's exact line ('Are you soliciting a bribe from me?') mirrors Stanford's line to Frank at 14:49, completing the symmetry. The 'That's politics' refrain — used by every member of the gang throughout the episode to dismiss people — is now used by a corrupt cop to justify taking a bribe from Mac. The phrase has completed a full ironic circuit: from Dennis's cynical dismissal of Mac's firing, through multiple gang members using it as a power move, to the ultimate authority figure (police) using it to solicit corruption. The episode's satirical thesis — that politics IS just corruption, as the gang cynically believed at the start — is validated in the most satisfying structural way. The economy is perfect (four words), the callback depth is maximum, and the thematic resonance is genuine. This earns its near-perfect score.

tmdb_overview: Driven by Frank's insight into the world of politics, Dennis pursues a political career by running for office.
